Restoring the community orchard

The community orchard reopened on Saturday after a year of restoration. Volunteers repaired the paths and planted apple trees beside the old stone wall. The project preserves a place where neighbors have gathered for generations.

A careful survey

Before planting began, the team measured soil moisture at twelve locations. They recorded each result in a shared notebook and compared the measurements with observations from the previous spring. The survey helped identify patches that needed better drainage.

Orchard coordinator Mira Patel said, “We wanted the old trees to thrive. New planting alone would not achieve that.” The volunteers kept the mature trees and cleared invasive plants by hand.

Work and observations

The first workday focused on paths and fences. Later sessions addressed soil health, watering, and pruning. Participants documented their work so that next year's volunteers could understand what had changed and why.

  • Inspect the watering system before each session.
  • Record observations in the public notebook.

The counts describe new trees only. Existing trees were surveyed separately, and the organizers cautioned that survival rates would need to be checked after the first summer. These observations are preliminary rather than a forecast.

What happens next

Volunteers will return every month to inspect the paths and water young trees. Residents can read the full restoration report before joining a workday. The report includes the survey method, equipment list, and notes from each session.
